There was never legislation to " keep these ships at least 230 miles away from U.S. coastlines."

The regulation created Emission Control Areas and stipulates that ships must burn fuel with 0.1% sulphur content starting 230 miles out. North Europe has similar rules and more countries with major ports are either considering the same or waiting to announce an implementation date.

At the same time many ports are upgrading their infrastructure to use "cold-ironing" while ships are in port. Previously, they had to keep their engines running to maintain power. Now they'll be able to shut the engines off and run off electricity. It's still relatively new but should be standard within the next decade, or maybe longer for smaller ports.

You can't just mandate 100% low sulphur fuel. Shipping is a very low margin industry and the cost impact to use only low sulphur instead of heavy fuel oil would be massive. And that's with demand relatively low. More regulations means higher demand and no one is sure how refineries would adjust to suddenly increased demand.

This is why I try not to suggest Antergos or Manjaro to new users. If I suggest an Arch-like distro, I suggest Arch and nothing else. I know that sounds elitist, but I have (in my mind) a good reason for that: Arch requires you to know exactly what's happening with your system, and this means you have some sort of idea what's going on when you do things... but Antergos/Manjaro take this detailed working-knowledge away from the user, while allowing updates that may break your system... meaning your system could break with new updates, but you're not familiar enough with your system to fix it. Please read my link, where I go into this with a little more detail and with some examples.

For example, I'm willing to bet your fan was running on high because of frequency scaling. I want to say that Antergos pegs your CPU as high as it'll go, and doesn't scale it in any way unless you set it to do otherwise. This'll cause excess heat, and therefore your fan will run at max until that heat goes down... but your processor isn't going to back off, so this'll never happen.

Your automatic network settings are turned off by default in Arch (not sure about Antergos), but I'm not sure where Antergos tells you about this... but Arch tells you RIGHT in their install process.

To set up automatic connections, you must run ip a and take note of your wired and wireless connections (wired starts with "e" and wireless starts with "w" -- my wired is "enp1s0" and my wireless is "wlp2s0", and yours should be structured something like that).

For a wired connection, find the ethernet-dhcp example in /etc/netctl/examples and copy it to /etc/netctl then edit the connection file you just copied to match your "e" connection you just found and took note of.

For a wireless connection, find the appropriate wireless connection in the examples folder and copy it the same way. Again, edit it and add your "w" connection you just took note of.

To switch automatically, run $ pacman -S ifplugd wpa_actiond and let that install. Once it's done, run netctl-ifplugd@[e-connection].service and netctl-auto@[w-connection].service. This should get you up and running, and automatically connect to any wired and wireless networks you have set up in your /etc/netctl/ folder.

So, mine would loo like:

$ systemctl start netctl-ifplugd@enp1s0.service

$ systemctl enable netctl-ifplugd@enp1s0.service

$ systemctl start netctl-auto@wlp2s0.service

$ systemctl enable netctl-auto@wlp2s0.service
